brand.source: Giltrap house steel blue and charcoal; the group's identity is deliberately marque-neutral, so no marque trade dress appears anywhere on this page

metaphor.sentence: A car is a thousand parts that only mean something in order — and so is a reply about one.

proposition: While the customer waits for a human to reply, assembling does the work the reply needs — so the person who answers is saying yes to a finished thing, not starting one.

wait.moment: the gap between an online enquiry and a human reply

duration.source: no NZ dealer group publishes its enquiry reply time
duration.note: The wait is real — enquiries arrive at 9pm, showrooms answer at 9am. No published NZ figure exists, so this page does not invent one.

wait.whyItExists: An enquiry needs a person who knows the car, and the car is one of thousands across twenty-four marques. Finding the right person with the right stock takes time the customer spends in silence.
wait.todayItFeelsLike: You ask about a specific car at 9pm. Somebody opens the inbox tomorrow. By then you are three tabs further down the road.

asks: One question, sized for a tap — “Is there a trade-in?”
“Weekday or weekend for a look in person?”
learns: Which car, exactly — not the model line, the VIN on the lot.
Whether the enquiry is tonight-serious or someday-curious, from what was asked.
What the trade-in is, if there is one, so the valuation can start now.
prepares: The reply, drafted from live stock — the car's actual history, actual location, actual availability.
The trade-in valuation request, queued for the buyer's own marque team.
The follow-up if this car sells first: the two closest cars actually on the lot.
resolves: The availability question — checked against the DMS, not memory.
The double-handling — the enquiry reaches one person, once, with everything attached.

reward.headline: An answer about the actual car, while you still care.
reward.detail: The reply that arrives is about the car you asked about — its real history, whether it is really available, what a look at it would take — with a person's name on it. If there is a trade-in, its valuation is already moving.

permission.consent: The customer asked about a car. That is the whole basis — the agent works that enquiry and nothing else.
reads: The group stock file, via the DMS
The enquired vehicle's history and media
The enquiry exactly as the customer wrote it
hardStops: It never sends anything a person has not approved.
It never changes a price or lists a vehicle.
It never contacts a customer on its own.
permission.retention: Drafts live in the DMS like any other note. Deleting the enquiry deletes the work.

human.gateAt: before anything is sent or published

primary.metric: enquiries answered while the customer is still looking
primary.mechanism: The reply is drafted from live stock the moment the enquiry lands, so the wait for a person is the wait for a yes — not for the work.

secondary.mechanism: Campaigns assemble from what is actually in stock, so nothing advertises a car that sold on Tuesday.

evidencePack.example: DMS stock record, vehicle history file, the enquiry as written
trade-in valuation is indicative until sighted; availability held for 48 hours
the dealer principal added a Saturday viewing slot before approving
S. Kenchington, Dealer Principal — 8:41am, before the reply went out

persona.name: Tom
persona.context: Asked about a specific used wagon at 9:12pm on a Sunday. Trade-in undeclared.

steps.showsCustomer: Got your message about the wagon. The showroom is closed — a person will reply in the morning. While you wait, two quick questions will make their answer better.
steps.doesBehind: Reads the enquiry and pulls the exact vehicle's record from the DMS: history, location, availability. Nothing is sent to anyone yet.
steps.question: Happy to answer two quick questions?

steps.showsCustomer: Is there a car you'd trade in? If there is, its valuation can start tonight instead of after your first visit.
steps.doesBehind: A declared trade-in goes to the right marque team's queue now. This is the single question that most often saves a second visit.
steps.question: Trading something in?

steps.showsCustomer: The wagon is at the Grey Lynn site and available. Weekday or weekend, if you wanted to see it?
steps.doesBehind: Availability is checked against the DMS, not somebody's memory of the lot. The answer is written down so nobody asks it again.
steps.question: When suits a look?

steps.showsCustomer: Putting the morning's reply together. Nothing sends without a person.
steps.doesBehind: Drafts the reply from the vehicle's real record, attaches the viewing options, and queues the trade-in valuation request. All of it sits as drafts in the DMS.

steps.approving: the reply, the viewing offer and the valuation request — before anything reaches the customer
steps.showsCustomer: Your reply is drafted and waiting for the morning's sign-off. A person sends it — that is the house rule, not a formality.
steps.doesBehind: Everything stops. The agent has no authority past this line.
steps.question: It's 8:40am. Release the drafts to the dealer principal?

steps.showsCustomer: Reply sent, 8:41am — the actual car, a Saturday slot, and your trade-in's indicative range. Here is everything that was done overnight, and who signed it.
steps.doesBehind: Writes the evidence pack: what was read, what was drafted, what the dealer principal changed, and the signature.

evidence.claim: New Zealanders spent 22 million hours on hold in 2025 — 8.7 hours each. Nearly half say slow service is reason enough to switch.
evidence.soWhat: The enquiry wait is the same wait in another channel. The customer who hears back first is the customer who visits.

evidence.claim: AI-referred traffic to retail sites grew 393% in a year, and it converts better than any other channel.
evidence.source: Adobe Digital Insights, quarterly AI traffic report, April 2026 — a US figure, flagged as such
evidence.soWhat: The buyer's agent is already shopping. A lot whose stock is current and readable is a lot that agents can recommend.

evidence.claim: Making the work visible increases how much people value the result — across five experiments, users preferred a slower service that showed its effort.
evidence.source: Buell & Norton, “The Labor Illusion”, Management Science 57(9)
evidence.soWhat: An overnight wait that shows its overnight work is worth more than a fast reply that shows nothing.

evidence.claim: A tribunal held an airline liable for what its chatbot told a customer, rejecting the argument that the chatbot was a separate legal entity.
evidence.soWhat: This is why the dealer principal gate exists. Nothing reaches a customer without a person who answers for it.

beforeWhileAfter.before: An enquiry lands in a shared inbox at 9pm. It reaches a salesperson when somebody sees it. The customer hears nothing until then, and some of them keep scrolling.
beforeWhileAfter.while: The agent reads the DMS, checks the car is really available, drafts the reply and starts the trade-in valuation — overnight, in the open, as drafts.
beforeWhileAfter.after: The dealer principal signs at 8:41am. The customer hears back about the actual car with a viewing slot attached — while they are still looking.

assemblyBeats.text: held — the dealer principal signs before it moves

explainer.heading: what a monetised wait state actually is
explainer.standfirst: Nobody has a word for this yet, so here it is drawn out. Four panels, about a minute.
explainer.definition: A monetised wait state is a wait that pays for itself — you get something useful out of it, and the business gets work done that would otherwise cost it money later.

panels.title: the wait you already have
panels.caption: Every dealer makes buyers wait somewhere. Here it is the overnight gap between an enquiry and a reply. Right now that gap produces nothing.

panels.title: what the gap costs
panels.caption: Some buyers keep scrolling. The ones who stay get asked the same questions twice. The valuation starts after the visit instead of before it.

panels.title: what fills it
panels.caption: assembling works the gap: two tap-sized questions in, a drafted reply and a moving valuation out — all of it sitting as drafts for the morning.

panels.title: who is better off
panels.caption: The buyer hears back about the actual car while they still care. The group answers once, with everything attached. The dealer principal signs every send.

textEquivalent: Start with the wait you already have. An enquiry about a car arrives at night; a person replies in the morning. Today, nothing happens in between.
That gap costs sales. Some buyers keep scrolling. The same questions get asked twice. The trade-in valuation starts a visit later than it could.
assembling fills the gap with useful work. It answers two tap-sized questions, drafts the reply from live stock, and starts the valuation — as drafts.

By morning, both sides are better off: the buyer gets an answer about the actual car with a viewing slot, and the group gets an enquiry handled once, completely. The dealer principal signs it, every time.
